newsitem.title: USA: Christopher Reeve pushes health insurance changes.
newsitem.headline: Christopher Reeve pushes health insurance changes.

text.p: Paralysed actor Christopher Reeve campaigned in Congress on Thursday for a bill that would lift a $1 million cap on health insurance policies and protect people like him from exhausting their health coverage when they need it most.

Reeve, paralysed from the neck down in a horse-riding accident two years ago, endorsed a bill that would raise the lifetime limit from $1 million to $10 million. The $1 million level, introduced in the 1970s, has been eroded by health care inflation.

A similar bill was defeated last year. But sponsors Sen. Jim Jeffords, a Vermont Republican who chairs the Labour and Human Resources committee, and Jay Rockefeller, a West Virginia Democrat, said they made changes to the bill in an effort to win more votes this year.
The new version exempts businesses with fewer than 20 employees and phases in the new cap by 2002. Rockefeller said it would increase the cost of insurance by less than half of one percent.

Former White House press secretary James Brady, wheelchair bound since he was injured in an assassination attempt on President Ronald Reagan in 1981, also backed the insurance measure and praised Reeve, who appeared in "Superman" films and is now a respected champion for the disabled.

"He has taught us more in the last two years about learning to soar than he ever did wearing tights," he joked at a news conference also attended by several families whose children risk using up all their coverage for treatment for diseases such as haemophilia or congenital heart defects.
Earlier on Thursday, Reeve addressed a Senate appropriations subcommittee, urging them to devote more money to research on brain and spinal cord injuries.
"We must not stop this progress because we are unwilling to commit enough money to get the job done," he said.
An accomplished rider, Reeve suffered multiple injuries including two shattered neck vertebrae when he was thrown from his horse at an equestrian event in Virginia in 1995.
Last month he told CBS News "48 Hours" he had started to regain feeling in his arms, hands and back.

During his stage and screen career, Reeve was best known for the "Superman" films based on the comic-book hero. Since his accident, Reeve has directed a television movie, appeared at the Academy Awards and the Democratic Party's national convention, as well as campaigned for the disabled.
